history.content: is the purple weed just a nutrient deficiency problem

draws.answer: It is not a nutrient deficiency problem, it is a nitrogen shortage disease. The signs are yellowing of lower leaves first, from the bottom up, with no spots, no streaks and no dead-heart, and it follows rain on a dry plot. That pattern is a sign of nitrogen being washed away, not a disease. Because it is a real disease you need to act on the whole plot, not only a low area, and you should avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK product or a systemic fungicide. Bring organic matter back first by applying manure, compost, or leaving residues unburned. Then use a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, go to ICAT.

history.content: movement restriction during outbreak now

history.content: There is a strange purple weed around the base of my sorghum and the crop is not growing well. What steps do I take?

draws.answer: You describe a purple weed growing around the base of your sorghum and the crop is not thriving. This weed problem is not covered in my training, and I will not suggest a cause, pest or product from a guess, as a wrong name could mislead you. Begin by checking the crop's environment: look for any tiny insects, weeds or dead plants on the ground, and note if the weed appears near the roots or the soil surface. Then look at the plants themselves, noting the colour of any marks and whether the damage is isolated or spread. Pull a few plants with roots, place them in a bag with some leaves, and leave them in the shade for a few hours. Do not spray anything until you have a sample. Take the plants and your notes to the ICAT extension service, which can look at the field.

history.content: why sorghum stays stunted yellow

draws.answer: The yellowing of the lower leaves while the top leaves remain green signals nitrogen deficiency from depleted organic matter. First, recognize the uniform pale colour as a sign of nitrogen hunger, not a disease, so fungicide will not help. Second, avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's suggestion because mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay back on run-down soil. Third, restore organic matter by applying manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, contact ICAT for a soil analysis and the proper fertilizer dose for your plot.

The yellowing makes the maize look dull and short, and the maize itself does not grow. Sorghum is a hungry crop that consumes a lot of nitrogen, so when it is short of nitrogen it leaves the older leaves behind, creating that yellowing while the younger leaves stay green. The uniform pale yellow on the older leaves signals nitrogen hunger, not a disease, so a fungicide will not work. First, read the leaves: the uniform pale colour is hunger for nitrogen, not a pathogen. Second, rebuild organic matter by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues unburnt. Third, rotate with a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Fourth, buy a soil check and the appropriate fertilizer from ICAT. I cannot give you a precise fertilizer dose without that check.

history.content: My goats have a mucky discharge from their eyes and some are dying quickly. What steps must I take?

draws.answer: Those signs are typical of leucaena poisoning caused by feeding too much leucaena. Cut the leucaena back so it forms only about a quarter to a third of the total ration. Mix it with grasses and cereal residues to provide sufficient roughage. Change the feed composition gradually over several days, not all at once. Give the animals clean water and a mineral or salt source at all times. If the animal continues to lose appetite, keeps drooling, or shows a swollen throat, consult the veterinary service.

Never use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service will provide the appropriate medication.

history.content: how far should fields be spaced to avoid spread

draws.answer: Spacing is not given in the brochure, and the catalogue's instruction is the spacing for the alley cropping one hectare of cowpea, which is 2 m by 2 m. After you finish the application, do a weeding round-up to keep the field tidy. If you later notice any streaks or dead-hearts, see ICAT.

history.content: I have sorghum that stays short and yellow, and a purple weed clings to its base, what is the cause?

draws.answer: Your sorghum is suffering from a nitrogen shortage on soil that has lost organic matter. First, look at the leaves; the uniform pale yellow on older lower leaves shows the plant is hungry for nitrogen, not a disease. Second, avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word because mineral fertilizer alone often does not give a return on depleted soil. Third, restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, rotate with a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, contact ICAT for a soil analysis and the proper dose for your plot.
